Gubernatorial A retired Justice of the Court of Appeal, Oludotun Adefope-Okojie
A retired Justice of the Court of Appeal, Oludotun Adefope-Okojie, has urged Nigerian courts to hold political parties accountable when they violate their constitutions or electoral laws, warning that party autonomy should not protect unlawful decisions from judicial scrutiny.
She also cautioned judges against declaring candidates who did not win elections as winners, saying courts should not take over the power of voters to choose their leaders.
Ms Adefope-Okojie spoke on Tuesday in Lagos while delivering the annual lecture of Gavel International, titled Electoral Process in Nigeria: Managing the Boundaries of Judicial Intervention.
“The courts must no longer refuse to intervene where political parties violate their own constitution and ‘rubbish’ the Electoral Act. They must intervene to sanitise the system,” she stated.
The chairman of the event, Anthony George-Ikoli, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), said the judiciary must protect electoral integrity without assuming the responsibilities of voters or electoral bodies.
“The judiciary must neither become an alternative electoral commission nor abdicate its responsibility as the ultimate guardian of electoral legality. That is the delicate boundary we are here this morning to interrogate,” he said.
Mr George-Ikoli said courts must be prepared to address unlawful conduct without exceeding their constitutional responsibilities.

“Judicial restraint should not amount to judicial retreat, just as judicial courage should not degenerate into overreach,” he said.
He added that an election could not be considered credible simply because a winner had emerged, but because the process that produced the winner could withstand legal scrutiny.
Ms Adefope-Okojie stated that the 1,209 petitions filed after Nigeria’s 2023 general elections reflected the level of distrust in the electoral process.
The petitions involved 1,280 elective positions, amounting to about 94.5 petitions for every 100 positions contested. Some seats attracted multiple petitions.
Comparing Nigeria’s experience with other countries, she said Zambia recorded about 83 parliamentary petitions after its 2021 elections for 156 seats, while Malawi had 44 petitions for 193 seats following its 2019 elections.
Kenya recorded 388 petitions involving 1,882 elective positions after its 2017 elections. The figure dropped to 123 after the 2022 elections, representing about 6.5 petitions per 100 seats. Ghana recorded 16 petitions for 275 parliamentary seats after its 2020 elections.
She also cited figures from the United Kingdom, South Africa and the United States. The UK recorded 302 petitions across parliamentary, European and local elections between 1900 and 2016. South Africa received 579 objections to its Electoral Commission after the 2024 elections, while the US recorded 756 election-related cases in 2023 and 2024, most concerning pre-election rules.
She acknowledged that the figures covered different categories of disputes and were not directly comparable.
“These figures do not measure the quality of justice. They measure trust, and on that measure the Nigerian electoral process is in severe deficit,” she said.
Ms Adefope-Okojie pointed to Kenya’s reduction in election petitions as an example of how stronger electoral institutions and effective dispute-resolution mechanisms could ease the burden on courts.
She urged Nigeria to improve the handling of disputes within political parties and at the electoral commission level so that more disagreements could be resolved before they reach election tribunals.
A report by the Policy and Legal Advocacy Centre (PLAC), From Ballot to the Courts: Analysis of Election Petition Litigation from Nigeria’s 2023 General Elections, also examined the outcome of the disputes.
PLAC analysed 1,503 court records, comprising 895 Election Petition Tribunal judgments, 588 Court of Appeal judgments and 20 Supreme Court judgements.
At the tribunal stage, 99 petitions succeeded, while 794 were dismissed. The Court of Appeal allowed 115 appeals and dismissed 446.
PLAC also identified 43 cases in which petitioners won at both the tribunal and appeal stages. Another 42 petitioners lost at the tribunal but succeeded on appeal, while 30 who initially won at the tribunal lost their cases on appeal.
The organisation stated that 4.8 per cent of the tribunal petitions analysed resulted in victories that were sustained through the appeal stage.
It found that the ability of petitioners to establish their cases with credible and admissible evidence determined the outcome of about 73 per cent of the petitions examined. Failure to meet mandatory procedural requirements accounted for 14.7 per cent, lack of jurisdiction for 8.5 per cent and lack of legal standing for 3.7 per cent.
Ms Adefope-Okojie said political parties could not rely on the principle of internal autonomy to justify actions that violated their constitutions or electoral laws.
She cited the Supreme Court’s decision in PDP v Alhaji Sule Lamido, Appeal No. SC/CV/164/2026, delivered on 30 April 2026.
The case followed Mr Lamido’s attempt to obtain a nomination form to contest for the position of national chairman of the Peoples Democratic Party at its 2025 national convention.
In a split 3-2 decision, the Supreme Court held that although courts generally avoid interfering in the internal affairs of political parties, they could intervene where a party violated its constitution or acted contrary to the law.
Justice Stephen Jonah Adah led the majority, alongside Justices Tsammani and Abubakar Sadiq Umar. Two justices dissented.
Ms Adefope-Okojie supported the majority decision, arguing that courts should not turn away from alleged violations simply because they concern the internal affairs of political parties.
She also referred to Zamfara APC v Marafa, the Bayelsa governorship dispute involving the PDP and Degi-Eremienyo, and the Plateau election disputes as examples of the consequences of unlawful party decisions and nomination processes.
The issue is particularly relevant under the Electoral Act 2026, which was signed into law on 18 February and repealed the 2022 Act.
Section 83(5) bars suits concerning the internal affairs of political parties, while Section 88(2) allows an aspirant to approach the Federal High Court where a party fails to comply with the Act or its nomination guidelines in selecting or nominating a candidate.
Section 85 also places limits on the criteria parties may use in selecting candidates.
The retired judge identified four approaches to electoral justice: corrective, protective, substitutive and abdicative.
She explained that corrective justice involves restoring a lawful vote or correcting an electoral wrong, while protective justice may require a fresh election where the original process cannot produce a reliable result.
Substitutive justice occurs when a court declares a candidate who did not receive the voters’ mandate as the winner. Abdicative justice, meanwhile, arises when a court refuses to examine credible allegations of malpractice because of procedural or evidential obstacles.
“No longer should an election be upheld in favour of a person the electorate did not vote for. The matter must be returned to the electorate for their own choice. Their choice must not be hijacked by the substitution of non-deserving candidates.”
Where a candidate’s qualification is defective but the lawful votes cannot establish who actually won, she said, a fresh election may be more appropriate than declaring the runner-up the winner.
“The test of a good election judgment is not only whether it applies the law correctly, but whether, at the end of it, the person who holds office is the person the lawful votes chose, or, if that cannot be known, whether the choice has been returned to the voters,” she said.
She cited Kenya’s Raila Odinga v IEBC judgment in 2017, in which the Supreme Court nullified the presidential election and ordered a fresh poll within 60 days.
She also referred to Malawi’s Mutharika v Chilima and Chakwera case, which led to the annulment of the 2019 presidential election and a rerun.
Other cases from Ghana, South Africa, India, the United States and the United Kingdom illustrated how courts in different jurisdictions have handled election disputes.
Ms Adefope-Okojie said the difficulty of proving electoral malpractice remained a major obstacle for petitioners.
She noted that petitioners were often required to establish irregularities polling unit by polling unit and show that the alleged breaches substantially affected the election result. With about 176,000 polling units across the country, meeting that requirement could be difficult.
She cited the Edo State governorship election petition filed by Asue Ighodalo of the PDP against Monday Okpebholo of the APC after the 2024 election.
The tribunal dismissed the petition, citing shortcomings in the evidence presented. The decision was subsequently upheld by the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court.
The retired judge questioned aspects of the treatment of documentary evidence, particularly the requirement for petitioners to call witnesses to establish the contents of public documents.
She referred to Sections 102 to 105 of the Evidence Act, which provide for the admissibility of public documents, including certified copies.
She also cited Paragraph 46(4) of the First Schedule to the Electoral Act 2026, which allows documentary evidence to be tendered and taken as read, with counsel addressing the court on its contents.
She urged judges to give proper consideration to admissible documentary evidence rather than reject it simply because the person who produced or certified it was not called to testify.
She also raised concerns about the difficulty petitioners face in securing the attendance of electoral officials as witnesses.
Since the Independent National Electoral Commission is often a respondent in election petitions, she said, its officials might be reluctant to testify against the commission unless compelled to do so.
She called for amendments to Paragraphs 4(5) and 4(6) of the First Schedule to the Electoral Act to exempt subpoenaed witnesses from the requirement to frontload witness statements.
She further urged clearer rules on electronic evidence, particularly the use of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV).
According to her, the undefined use of the expression “communication failure” could create uncertainty in disputes involving electronic transmission of results and undermine confidence in the electoral process.
The concerns come as the judiciary prepares for another round of election disputes ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027, while governorship and State House of Assembly elections will be held on 6 February.
At a meeting with election tribunal judges on 10 November, the Chief Justice of Nigeria, Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, and the Attorney-General of the Federation, Lateef Fagbemi, warned judicial officers against political interference, intimidation and inducement.
The President of the Court of Appeal, Monica Dongban-Mensem, said 375 judicial officers had been nominated to serve on election petition tribunals, comprising 237 new members and 138 returning members.
INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan also identified disputes over electronic transmission of results, BVAS, IReV, party primaries and candidate nominations as likely sources of litigation after the elections.
The 2023 elections placed considerable demands on the judiciary. In September 2023, Ms Dongban-Mensem said 98 panels were required to handle the 1,209 petitions filed after the polls.
Ms Adefope-Okojie urged the Chief Justice of Nigeria, the President of the Court of Appeal and other heads of courts to appoint judges of proven integrity and political neutrality to election tribunals.
“The Constitution places sovereignty in the people and makes the Courts the guardians of that sovereignty, not its holders,” she said.
She said the ultimate goal should be a credible electoral process in which voters determine the winners and fewer disputes require judicial intervention.
“The final aim of electoral adjudication should be its own decline: a democracy in which elections are won and lost at the ballot box, not in the courtroom.”
